newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila denies IMF directive on real estate loans.
newsitem.headline: Manila denies IMF directive on real estate loans.

text.p: Philippine Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson on Monday denied reports the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had required banks to limit their loan exposures to real estate companies.

Singson's statement came after local newspapers said the Philippine government was considering a specific provision in the country's IMF exit programme limiting to a maximum of 30 percent the real estate loan portfolio of banks.
The reports said this was contained in a Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies (MEP) submitted by the Philippine government to an IMF team which recently visited the country.
Asked about the reports, the IMF's resident representative in Manila David Nellor told Reuters: "It's (the reports) not an accurate reflection of what is contained in the MEP."

He said the banks' property loan exposures was one of the policies discussed in the last review of the IMF. This was taken up in the light of strengthening the banking sector since real estate is a cyclical business, he added.

"I understand that they're (the Central Bank) considering other measures such as reducing the proportion of real estate valuation that can be used as collateral for loans and measures such as that would be seen as an important signal to the financial markets that the Central Bank is monitoring banks' exposure to the real estate sector closely," Nellor said.
Currently, property holdings can account for 70 percent of the collateral on a loan.
The exposure of Philippine banks to real estate loans caused some concern last year after analysts said a cooling down in the booming property market could hit banks.

The IMF team ended its review in February and a finalised memorandum was expected to be circulated to the IMF executive board at the beginning of this month. The Philippines is expected to exit from IMF supervision in late June this year.
In the same statement, Singson also said the Central Bank's manual of regulations already limited to 30 percent the maximum exposure that a bank may lend to any particular sector.
A study made by the Central Bank last year showed that the average loan portfolio of banks to the real estate sector was at 11 percent.
He added that the Central Bank was studying other options to limit banks' real estate exposure.
The study would determine whether the lending limits should be imposed on mass housing projects or it should be confined to high-rise buildings or condominiums, Singson said.
